items.story:
Japan is poised to introduce a significant change to its family law, with an amendment to the Civil Code set to allow shared parenting for the first time, potentially ending the practice of sole custody in divorce cases. The proposed law change has been welcomed by advocates for reform, who argue that it will help to reduce the trauma experienced by children when their parents divorce. Currently, Japanese family law typically grants sole custody to one parent, often the mother, following a divorce. This can lead to the other parent being cut out of their child's life, a situation that has been criticized for causing unnecessary distress to all parties involved.

The existing system has been in place for decades, with its roots in traditional Japanese family values and social norms. However, as societal attitudes towards family and relationships have evolved, so too have calls for reform of the country's family law.
